# Crank--Nicolson Method

## Biological problem

We consider a substance with concentration $u(x,t)$ that diffuses in one spatial dimension with a constant diffusion coefficient $D$. There are point-like agents that act as sources and sinks in this one-dimensional space. They may secrete the substance into the environment or remove it through uptake. These point-like agents might represent individual bacteria or discrete protein clusters positioned at specific locations along a filament or channel.

:::{.callout-note title="Dimensions and units"}

We use the following dimensions and units:

- $M$ denotes 'amount of substance' (e.g. units of moles, molecules, or mass).
- $L$ denotes the length (e.g. µm),
- $T$ denotes time (e.g. seconds).

Where dimension-generic expressions are given, $d$ denotes the number of spatial dimensions. For this document $d=1$.
:::



## Equation to solve

We now formalize this biological scenario as a partial differential equation. The governing diffusion--reaction equation is

$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}
=
D \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}
+
o(x)
-
r(x)\,u.
$$ {#eq-main}

Here,

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|---|---|---|
| $u(x,t)$ | Extracellular concentration | $M/L^d$ |
| $\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}$ | Second spatial derivative | $M/L^{d+2}$ |
| $D$ | Diffusion coefficient | $L^2/T$ |
| $o(x)$ | Source term (production of $u$) | $M/(L^d\,T)$ |
| $r(x)$ | per-agent uptake rate coefficient | $1/T$ |

Let $B_o$ denote the set of secreting agents and $B_i$ the set of consuming agents, and let $x_s$ be the position of agent $s$. The agents are represented as a point-like source rate $o(x)$ and a point-like per-agent uptake rate $r(x)$ using Dirac delta functions:

$$
o(x)
=
K_o
\sum_{s\in B_o}
\delta(x-x_s),
$$

$$
r(x)
=
K_r
\sum_{s\in B_i}
\delta(x-x_s).
$$

with the following parameters:

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|---|---|---|
| $K_o$ | Per-agent secretion rate (point-source strength) | $M/T$ |
| $K_r$ | Per-agent first-order uptake coefficient | $L^d/T$ |


## Module structure

Before deriving the numerical method, we outline the software components that will implement it. We want to build a TypeScript module `crankNicolson.ts` that will numerically solve @eq-main. The module will consist of three major parts: @lst-global-variables, @lst-cn-set-parameters, and @lst-cn-time-stepping, as shown below:

```{.typescript #lst-crankNicolson lst-cap=lst-crankNicolson file=src/crankNicolson.ts filename="src/crankNicolson.ts"}

<<lst-global-variables>>

<<lst-cn-set-parameters>>

<<lst-cn-time-stepping>>
```

All code blocks shown in this chapter will be contained in either of these three parts. This way, in @lst-global-variables we will store module-level variables and arrays that persist across time steps. In @lst-cn-set-parameters we will expose a function that someone can use to initiate the solver with their particular equation parameters and discretization grid, or update the positions of agents that may move during the simulation. The main time-stepping loop will be in @lst-cn-time-stepping, this function will update the concentration by one or more time steps using the Thomas algorithm to solve the tridiagonal system.



## Discrete Approximation

To solve @eq-main numerically, we first discretize space and time onto a finite grid.


```{ojs}
//|echo: false
d3 = require("d3@7")

drawGrid = (N,highlightCell) => {
    const width = 420, height = 240;
    const marginX = 60;

    // Each entry is a cell index (or null for the elided gap between shown cells).
    // Cell i occupies [i, i+1] and is sampled at its midpoint i+0.5 — cell-centered.
    const cellIndices = (() => {
      if (N <= 5) {
        return d3.range(N);
      }
      return [0, 1, 2, null, N - 2, N - 1];
    })();

    const displayItems = cellIndices.map(i => {
      if (i === null) {
        return { type: "dots" };
      }

      return {
        type: "node",
        i,
        x: i + 0.5,
        indexLabel:
          N > 5 && i === N - 2
            ? "i = N-2"
            : N > 5 && i === N - 1
            ? "i = N-1"
            : "i = "+String(i)
      };
    });

  const nodeItems = displayItems.filter(d => d.type === "node");

  // Cell-boundary tick marks: every integer boundary adjacent to a shown cell.
  const boundarySet = new Set();
  nodeItems.forEach(d => { boundarySet.add(d.i); boundarySet.add(d.i + 1); });
  const boundaries = Array.from(boundarySet).sort((a, b) => a - b);


  const yN  = 90;  // baseline for time level n
  const yN1 = 190; // baseline for time level n+1

  const x = d3.scaleLinear()
      .domain([0, N])
      .range([marginX, width - marginX]);

  const svg = d3.create("svg")
      .attr("width", width)
      .attr("height", height);

  svg.append("defs").append("marker")
      .attr("id", "arrow")
      .attr("viewBox", "0 0 10 10")
      .attr("refX", 5).attr("refY", 5)
      .attr("markerWidth", 6).attr("markerHeight", 6)
      .attr("orient", "auto-start-reverse")
    .append("path")
      .attr("d", "M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 Z")
      .attr("fill", "gray");

  // Shade one cell's full width to make clear a grid point represents a whole
  // cell, sampled at its center, not a single physical point.
  [yN, yN1].forEach(y => {
    svg.append("rect")
        .attr("x", x(highlightCell))
        .attr("width", x(highlightCell + 1) - x(highlightCell))
        .attr("y", y - 21)
        .attr("height", 42)
        .attr("fill", "#4C78A8")
        .attr("fill-opacity", 0.12);
  });

  function drawRow(y, label) {
    const safeId = label.replace("+", "");

    svg.append("line")
        .attr("x1", x(0)).attr("x2", x(N))
        .attr("y1", y).attr("y2", y)
        .attr("stroke", "black")
        .attr("stroke-width", 1.5);

    svg.selectAll(`line.tick-${safeId}`)
      .data(boundaries)
      .join("line")
        .attr("class", `tick-${safeId}`)
        .attr("x1", b => x(b)).attr("x2", b => x(b))
        .attr("y1", y - 8).attr("y2", y + 8)
        .attr("stroke", "black")
        .attr("stroke-width", 1);

    svg.selectAll(`circle.row-${safeId}`)
      .data(nodeItems)
      .join("circle")
        .attr("class", `row-${safeId}`)
        .attr("cx", d => x(d.x))
        .attr("cy", y)
        .attr("r", 6)
        .attr("fill", "grey");

    svg.append("text")
        .attr("x", marginX - 25)
        .attr("y", y + 4)
        .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
        .attr("font-weight", "bold")
        .text(label);
  }
  drawRow(yN, "n");
  drawRow(yN1, "n+1");

  displayItems.forEach(d => {
    if (d.type === "node") {
      svg.append("text")
        .attr("x", x(d.x))
        .attr("y", yN - 22)
        .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
        .attr("font-size", "14px")
        .text(d.indexLabel);
    } else {
      svg.append("text")
        .attr("x", (x(3) + x(N - 2)) / 2)
        .attr("y", yN - 22)
        .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
        .attr("font-size", "12px")
        .text("…");
    }
  });

  nodeItems.forEach(d => {
    svg.append("line")
        .attr("x1", x(d.x)).attr("x2", x(d.x))
        .attr("y1", yN + 9).attr("y2", yN1 - 9)
        .attr("stroke", "lightgray")
        .attr("stroke-dasharray", "3,3");
  });

  svg.append("line")
      .attr("x1", marginX - 25).attr("x2", marginX - 25)
      .attr("y1", yN + 15).attr("y2", yN1 - 15)
      .attr("stroke", "gray")
      .attr("marker-end", "url(#arrow)")
      .attr("marker-start", "url(#arrow)");

  svg.append("text")
      .attr("x", marginX - 45)
      .attr("y", (yN + yN1) / 2 + 4)
      .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
      .text("Δt");

  svg.append("line")
      .attr("x1", x(highlightCell)).attr("x2", x(highlightCell + 1))
      .attr("y1", yN - 40).attr("y2", yN - 40)
      .attr("stroke", "gray")
      .attr("marker-end", "url(#arrow)")
      .attr("marker-start", "url(#arrow)");

  svg.append("text")
      .attr("x", (x(highlightCell) + x(highlightCell + 1)) / 2)
      .attr("y", yN - 42)
      .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
      .text("Δx");

  const xMinLabel = svg.append("text")
      .attr("x", x(0))
      .attr("y", yN + 125)
      .attr("text-anchor", "middle");
  xMinLabel.append("tspan").text("x");
  xMinLabel.append("tspan")
      .attr("dy", "0.25em")
      .attr("font-size", "0.7em")
      .text("min");

const x2Label = svg.append("text")
      .attr("x", (x(highlightCell) + x(highlightCell + 1)) / 2)
      .attr("y", yN + 125)
      .attr("text-anchor", "middle");
  x2Label.append("tspan").text("x");
  x2Label.append("tspan")
      .attr("dy", "0.25em")
      .attr("font-size", "0.7em")
      .text(String(highlightCell));


  svg.append("text")
      .attr("x", width / 2)
      .attr("y", 15)   // was 20
      .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
      .attr("font-weight", "bold")
      .text("Crank–Nicolson space–time grid");

  const container = document.createElement("div");
  container.style.textAlign = "center";
  container.appendChild(svg.node());
  return container;
}

schematicN6 = drawGrid(6,1) // number of cells, indices 0..5
```


Discretize the 1D space using a uniform grid of $N$ cells (`N`) with grid spacing $\Delta x$ (`dx`). The grid is cell-centered: cell $i$ represents the interval $[x_{\min}+i\Delta x,\,x_{\min}+(i+1)\Delta x]$ and is sampled at its midpoint,

$$
x_i = x_{\min} + (i+0.5) \Delta x \qquad i = 0, 1, \ldots, N-1,
$$

and discretize time by time-steps of length $\Delta t$ (`dt`)

$$
t^n = n \Delta t,
$$


then, the array $U^n$ (`U`) approximates $u$, storing the values $U_i^n$ (`U[i]`) where

$$
u(x_i,t^n)\approx U_i^n
$$

Approximate the Laplacian by

$$
\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}\biggr|_{(x_i,t^n)}
\approx
[\Delta U]_i^n
:=
\frac{U_{i-1}^n - 2U_i^n + U_{i+1}^n}{(\Delta x)^2}.
$$ {#eq-discrete-laplacian}

and approximate the time derivative at $(x_i,t^n)$ by


$$
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}
\biggr|_{(x_i,t^n)}
\approx
[D_t^+ U]_i^n
:=
\frac{U_i^{n+1} - U_i^n}{\Delta t}.
$$ {#eq-forward-time-difference}

The sources and sinks will be discretized as follows:
$$
o(x)
\biggr|_{(x_i)}
\approx
O_i
=
\frac{K_o}{\Delta x}
m_i^{o}
$$ {#eq-source-discrete}


$$
r(x)
\biggr|_{(x_i)}
\approx
R_i
=
\frac{K_r}{\Delta x}
m_i^{r}
$$ {#eq-sink-discrete}


```{.typescript #lst-compute-O-I lst-cap="lst-compute-O-I"}
const O_i = (K_o / dx) * mo[i];
const R_i = (K_r / dx) * mr[i];
```

where $m_i^{o}$ (`mo[i]`) and $m_i^{r}$ (`mr[i]`) denote the number of secreting and consuming agents in grid cell $i$, and let $i_s$ be the grid index of the cell to which agent $s$ is assigned (for example, the nearest grid cell)

$$
m_i^{o} = \sum_{s\in B_o} \delta_{i,i_s}, \qquad
m_i^{r} = \sum_{s\in B_i} \delta_{i,i_s},
$$ {#eq-agents-counts}

Here, $\delta_{i,i_s}$ is the Kronecker delta, which is dimensionless (unlike the Dirac delta $\delta(x)$ used in the continuous case, which has units of $1/L^d$).




The factor $1/\Delta x$ represents each point-like agent as a source or sink distributed over its assigned grid cell. Consequently, integrating the discrete source or sink over that cell recovers the secretion or uptake associated with that agent.


This way, we can write the discretized @eq-main at a particular grid cell $i$ and time step $n$ as

$$
[D_t^+U]_i^n = D [\Delta U]_i^n +O_i - R_i U_i^n
$${#eq-discrete}

## Setting parameters

With the discretization defined, we now build the function that configures the solver with the chosen grid and reaction parameters. All the parameters related to the discretization choices (`dx`, `dt`, and `N`), reaction rates (`K_o` and `K_r`) and diffusion rate (`D`) will be supplied to @lst-cn-set-parameters:

```{.typescript #lst-cn-set-parameters lst-cap="lst-define-cn-set-parameters"}

export const CNSetParameters = (
    numberOfGridPoints: number,
    D: number,
    dx: number,
    dt: number,
    K_r: number,
    K_o: number,
    mr: Float64Array,
    mo: Float64Array,
): void => {

	if (N !== numberOfGridPoints){

		  N = numberOfGridPoints;

		  <<lst-alloc-q-beta>>
		  <<lst-alloc-diagonals>>
		  <<lst-alloc-thomas-scratch-arrays>>
	}

	<<lst-compute-lambda>>
	<<lst-fill-q-beta>>
	<<lst-fill-diagonals>>

};
```
Notice that in the function `CNSetParameters()` we allocate arrays only if the number of grid cells `N` has changed or has not yet been initialized. As we will see, these arrays must have length `N`. If the number of grid points does not change between calls, all the arrays used in this module will get reused. For this reason `N` will be declared as a global variable in @lst-global-variables



```{.typescript #lst-global-variables lst-cap="lst-global-variables"}
import { thomasAlgorithm } from "./thomasAlgorithm.js";

let N: number = 0;

<<lst-declare-lambda-q-beta>>
<<lst-declare-diagonals>>
<<lst-declare-thomas-scratch-arrays>>
```




## Crank--Nicolson scheme

Having discretized space and time, we now introduce the Crank--Nicolson method to advance the concentration forward in time. Using the Crank--Nicolson method, the diffusion and reaction terms in @eq-discrete are averaged between time levels $n$ and $n+1$. The source rate $O_i$ and the uptake rate $R_i$ are constant within a single time step. Therefore $O_i$ is included directly (it has no $U$-dependence to average), while both the diffusion term $[\Delta U]_i$ and the uptake term $R_i U$ are time-averaged:


$$
[D_t^+ U]_i^n
=
\frac{D}{2}
\Bigl[
[\Delta U]_i^{n+1}
+
[\Delta U]_i^{n}
\Bigr] + O_i -
\frac{R_i}{2}
\left[
U_i^{n+1} + U_i^n
\right]
$$ {#eq-crank-nicolson}

Inserting @eq-discrete-laplacian and @eq-forward-time-difference into
@eq-crank-nicolson and multiplying by $\Delta t$, we arrive at the linear system


$$
\begin{aligned}
U_i^{n+1} - U_i^n
={}&
\frac{D \Delta t}{2 \Delta x^2}
\Bigl[
    U_{i-1}^{n+1}
    - 2U_i^{n+1}
    + U_{i+1}^{n+1}
    + U_{i-1}^{n}
    - 2U_i^{n}
    + U_{i+1}^{n}
\Bigr]
\\
&+
O_i \Delta t
\\
&-
\frac{R_i \Delta t}{2}
\Bigl[
    U_i^n + U_i^{n+1}
\Bigr]
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-crank-nicolson-expanded}


For convenience, define the parameters $\lambda$, $q_i$, and $\beta_i$:

$$
\lambda
=
\frac{D \Delta t}{2\Delta x^2}
\qquad
q_i=
O_i\,\Delta t,
\qquad
\beta_i
=
\frac{R_i\,\Delta t}{2}
$$

so that the equation can be written as


$$
\begin{aligned}
U_i^{n+1} - U_i^n
={}&
\lambda
\Bigl[
    U_{i-1}^{n+1}
    - 2U_i^{n+1}
    + U_{i+1}^{n+1}
    + U_{i-1}^{n}
    - 2U_i^{n}
    + U_{i+1}^{n}
\Bigr]
\\
&+ q_i \\
&-\beta_i
\Bigl[
    U_i^n + U_i^{n+1}
\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
$${#eq-row-i}

$\lambda$, $q$, and $\beta$ are declared as global variables in @lst-global-variables as

```{.typescript #lst-declare-lambda-q-beta lst-cap="lst-declare-lambda-q-beta"}
let lambda: number;
let q: Float64Array;
let beta: Float64Array;
```


The arrays `q` and `beta` are allocated with size `N` at @lst-cn-set-parameters

```{.typescript #lst-alloc-q-beta lst-cap="lst-alloc-q-beta"}
q = new Float64Array(N);
beta = new Float64Array(N);
```

The parameters `lambda` and the entries of `q`, and `beta` are then computed inside the same @lst-cn-set-parameters
as

```{.typescript #lst-compute-lambda lst-cap="lst-compute-lambda"}
lambda = (D * dt) / (2.0 * dx * dx);
```

and the arrays `q` and `beta` as

```{.typescript #lst-fill-q-beta lst-cap="lst-fill-q-beta"}
for (let i: number = 0; i < N; i++) {
  <<lst-compute-O-I>>
	q[i] = O_i * dt;
	beta[i] = (R_i * dt) / 2.0;
}
```
Here we used the previously computed `O_i` and `R_i` from @lst-compute-O-I



## Tridiagonal system

The Crank--Nicolson scheme yields a system of linear equations that we now rearrange into tridiagonal form. Collecting the unknown terms in @eq-row-i at time level $n+1$ on the left-hand side gives

$$
- \lambda U_{i-1}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_i\right) U_i^{n+1}
- \lambda U_{i+1}^{n+1}
=
 \lambda U_{i-1}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_i\right) U_i^n
+\lambda U_{i+1}^{n}
+q_i.
$$ {#eq-crank-nicolson-tridiagonal}

This equation applies to every interior grid cell $i=1,\ldots,N-2$, while the Neumann boundary condition is applied at the boundary cells $i=0$ and $i=N-1$. Because the grid is cell-centered, the zero-flux ghost value at each boundary equals the boundary cell's own value. This way, for a spatial domain with $N$ grid cells, we obtain a system of $N$ linear equations. The system can be written in matrix form as

$$
A U^{n+1} = d
$${#eq-matrix}

where $A$ is the $N \times N$ tridiagonal matrix

$$
A =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 + \lambda + \beta_0 & -\lambda & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
-\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_1 & -\lambda & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & -\lambda & \ddots & \ddots & 0 \\
\vdots & \ddots & \ddots & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_{N-2} & -\lambda \\
0 & \cdots & 0 & -\lambda & 1 + \lambda + \beta_{N-1}
\end{bmatrix},
$$

$U^{n+1}$ is the unknown vector of concentrations at time level $n+1$,

$$
U^{n+1} =
\begin{bmatrix}
U_0^{n+1} \\
U_1^{n+1} \\
\vdots \\
U_{N-2}^{n+1} \\
U_{N-1}^{n+1}
\end{bmatrix},
$$

and the right-hand side vector $d$ is given by

$$
d =
\begin{bmatrix}
\left(1 - \lambda - \beta_0\right) U_0^n + \lambda U_1^n + q_0 \\
\lambda U_0^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_1\right) U_1^n + \lambda U_2^n + q_1 \\
\vdots \\
\lambda U_{N-3}^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_{N-2}\right) U_{N-2}^n + \lambda U_{N-1}^n + q_{N-2} \\
\lambda U_{N-2}^n + \left(1 - \lambda - \beta_{N-1}\right) U_{N-1}^n + q_{N-1}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Here, the entries of $A$ and $d$ at the boundaries $i=0$ and $i=N-1$ incorporate Neumann (zero-flux) boundary conditions. 

The solution vector $U^{n+1}$ is solved from the system $A U^{n+1} = d$ using the Thomas algorithm, whose implementation lives in a separate module.



## Building the tridiagonal matrix $A$

We now implement the construction of the coefficient matrix $A$ from its three diagonals. The matrix $A$ is built from the lower, main, and upper diagonals.


The three diagonals are declared in @lst-global-variables as global variables


```{.typescript #lst-declare-diagonals lst-cap="lst-declare-diagonals"}
let lowerDiagonal: Float64Array;
let mainDiagonal: Float64Array;
let upperDiagonal: Float64Array;
```


The diagonals are allocated with size `N` in @lst-cn-set-parameters

```{.typescript #lst-alloc-diagonals lst-cap="lst-alloc-diagonals"}
lowerDiagonal = new Float64Array(N);
mainDiagonal = new Float64Array(N);
upperDiagonal = new Float64Array(N);
```

and then filled with their corresponding parameter values in the same @lst-cn-set-parameters:

```{.typescript #lst-fill-diagonals lst-cap="lst-fill-diagonals"}
lowerDiagonal.fill(-lambda)
lowerDiagonal[0] = 0.0;

upperDiagonal.fill(-lambda)
upperDiagonal[N - 1] = 0.0;

for (let i: number = 1; i < N - 1; i++) {
  mainDiagonal[i] = 1.0 + 2.0 * lambda + beta[i];
}
mainDiagonal[0] = 1.0 + lambda + beta[0];
mainDiagonal[N - 1] = 1.0 + lambda + beta[N - 1];

```

Notice that we set the first element of the lower diagonal and the last element of the upper diagonal to zero, since the corresponding off-domain grid cells ($i=-1$ and $i=N$) lie outside the computational domain.

## Building the right-hand side

With the matrix $A$ in place, we turn to constructing the right-hand side vector $d$. The entries of the right-hand side vector $d$ are given by @eq-crank-nicolson-tridiagonal. For interior grid points $i = 1,\ldots,N-2$, each entry is

$$
d_i = \lambda U_{i-1}^n + (1 - 2\lambda - \beta_i) U_i^n + \lambda U_{i+1}^n + q_i.
$$

To handle the Neumann (zero-flux) boundary conditions on this cell-centered grid, the ghost cell just outside the domain equals the boundary cell's own value: $U_{-1} = U_0$ at the left boundary and $U_N = U_{N-1}$ at the right boundary. Substituting $U_{-1}=U_0$ at $i=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
d_0
&= \lambda U_{-1}^n + (1 - 2\lambda - \beta_0) U_0^n + \lambda U_1^n + q_0 \\
&= (1 - \lambda - \beta_0) U_0^n + \lambda U_1^n + q_0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, at the right boundary ($i=N-1$), $U_N = U_{N-1}$, so

$$
d_{N-1} = (1 - \lambda - \beta_{N-1}) U_{N-1}^n + \lambda U_{N-2}^n + q_{N-1}.
$$

This boundary treatment is implemented directly in the code that builds $d$ at each time step inside @lst-cn-time-stepping

```{.typescript #lst-compute-rhs-vector lst-cap="lst-compute-rhs-vector"}

for (let i: number = 1; i < N - 1; i++) {
	d[i] = lambda * U[i - 1]
		+ (1.0 - 2.0 * lambda - beta[i]) * U[i]
		+ lambda * U[i + 1]
		+ q[i];
}

d[0] = (1.0 - lambda - beta[0]) * U[0]
	+ lambda * U[1]
	+ q[0];

d[N - 1] = (1.0 - lambda - beta[N - 1]) * U[N - 1]
	+ lambda * U[N - 2]
	+ q[N - 1];
```
Notice that, as long as the positions of the sinks and sources do not change, the three diagonals do not need to be recomputed. On the other hand, the vector $d$ has to be recomputed at every single time step, because it depends on the concentration from the previous step.

:::{.callout-note collapse=true title='Example for $N=5$ and Neumann BC'}

```{ojs}
//|code-fold: true
schematicN5 = drawGrid(5,2)
```

If we apply this equation to $5$ grid points ($i=0,1,2,3,4$), we obtain a system of $5$ linear equations for the unknowns $U_i^{n+1}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
-{\color{red} \lambda U_{-1}^{n+1}}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_0\right) U_0^{n+1}
- \lambda U_{1}^{n+1}
={}&
{\color{red} \lambda U_{-1}^{n}}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_0\right) U_0^n
+\lambda U_{1}^{n}
+q_0,
\\
- \lambda U_{0}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_1\right) U_1^{n+1}
- \lambda U_{2}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda U_{0}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_1\right) U_1^n
+\lambda U_{2}^{n}
+q_1,
\\
- \lambda U_{1}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_2\right) U_2^{n+1}
- \lambda U_{3}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda U_{1}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_2\right) U_2^n
+\lambda U_{3}^{n}
+q_2,
\\
- \lambda U_{2}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_3\right) U_3^{n+1}
 - \lambda U_{4}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda U_{2}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_3\right) U_3^n
+\lambda U_{4}^{n}
+q_3,
\\
 - \lambda U_{3}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_4\right) U_4^{n+1}
 - {\color{red} \lambda U_{5}^{n+1}}
={}&
 \lambda U_{3}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_4\right) U_4^n
+{\color{red}\lambda U_{5}^{n}}
+q_4.
\end{aligned}
$$
Here, the red terms correspond to cells outside the domain which represent the boundary conditions. These are set to the prescribed boundary values in the case of Dirichlet boundary conditions, or set via ghost-cell mirroring in the case of Neumann (zero-flux) boundary conditions. For this implementation, we use Neumann zero-flux boundary conditions on a cell-centered grid, so the ghost cell equals the boundary cell's own value: $U_{-1} = U_0$ at the left boundary and $U_{N} = U_{N-1}$ at the right boundary. This way, by setting $U_{-1} = U_0$ and $U_5 = U_4$, we can eliminate the red terms, giving

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(1 + \lambda + \beta_0\right) U_0^{n+1} - \lambda U_{1}^{n+1}
={}&
\left(1 - \lambda - \beta_0\right) U_0^n
+ \lambda U_{1}^{n}
+q_0,
\\
- \lambda U_{0}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_1\right) U_1^{n+1}
- \lambda U_{2}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda U_{0}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_1\right) U_1^n
+\lambda U_{2}^{n}
+q_1,
\\
- \lambda U_{1}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_2\right) U_2^{n+1}
- \lambda U_{3}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda U_{1}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_2\right) U_2^n
+\lambda U_{3}^{n}
+q_2,
\\
- \lambda U_{2}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + 2\lambda + \beta_3\right) U_3^{n+1}
- \lambda U_{4}^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda U_{2}^{n}
+\left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_3\right) U_3^n
+\lambda U_{4}^{n}
+q_3,
\\
- \lambda U_{3}^{n+1}
+ \left(1 + \lambda + \beta_4\right) U_4^{n+1}
={}&
 \lambda U_{3}^{n}
+\left(1 - \lambda - \beta_4\right) U_4^n
+q_4.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a tridiagonal system that can be represented in matrix form as $A U^{n+1} = d$, where $A$ is

$$
A =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 + \lambda + \beta_0 & -\lambda & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
-\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_1 & -\lambda & 0 & 0 \\
0 & -\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_2 & -\lambda & 0 \\
0 & 0 & -\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda + \beta_3 & -\lambda \\
0 & 0 & 0 & -\lambda & 1 + \lambda + \beta_4
\end{bmatrix},
$$

$U^{n+1}$ is

$$
U^{n+1} =
\begin{bmatrix}
U_0^{n+1} \\
U_1^{n+1} \\
U_2^{n+1} \\
U_3^{n+1} \\
U_4^{n+1}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

and the right-hand side vector $d$ is
$$
d =
\begin{bmatrix}
\left(1 - \lambda - \beta_0\right) U_0^n + \lambda U_1^n + q_0 \\
\lambda U_0^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_1\right) U_1^n + \lambda U_2^n + q_1 \\
\lambda U_1^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_2\right) U_2^n + \lambda U_3^n + q_2 \\
\lambda U_2^n + \left(1 - 2\lambda - \beta_3\right) U_3^n + \lambda U_4^n + q_3 \\
\lambda U_3^n + \left(1 - \lambda - \beta_4\right) U_4^n + q_4
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

:::



## Thomas algorithm

Now that the tridiagonal system is assembled, we solve it efficiently using the Thomas algorithm, a specialised form of Gaussian elimination for tridiagonal systems. This particular implementation requires as input parameters the three diagonals of matrix $A$, the right-hand side vector $d$, $N$, a buffer array `modifiedUpper` of length `N` and finally an array `U` where the algorithm will store the solution to $U^{n+1}$.

The Thomas algorithm modifies the right-hand side `d` in place during forward elimination and needs `modifiedUpper` as a scratch buffer for the modified upper diagonal. To avoid allocating these arrays on every time step — they live inside the hot loop — we pre-allocate them at module scope.

They are declared at @lst-global-variables as

```{.typescript #lst-declare-thomas-scratch-arrays lst-cap="lst-declare-thomas-scratch-arrays"}
let modifiedUpper: Float64Array;
let d: Float64Array;
```

They are allocated by `CNSetParameters` as

```{.typescript #lst-alloc-thomas-scratch-arrays lst-cap="lst-alloc-thomas-scratch-arrays"}
modifiedUpper = new Float64Array(N);
d = new Float64Array(N);
```

The time-stepping loop assembles the right-hand side and calls the Thomas algorithm, as shown in @lst-cn-time-stepping:

```{.typescript #lst-cn-time-stepping lst-cap="lst-define-cn-time-stepping"}

export const CNTimeStepping = (
    U: Float64Array,
    totalNumberOfIterations: number,
): void => {

  for (let step: number = 0; step < totalNumberOfIterations; step++) {

    <<lst-compute-rhs-vector>>

    thomasAlgorithm(
      lowerDiagonal,
      mainDiagonal,
      upperDiagonal,
      d,
      N,
      modifiedUpper,
      U,
    );

  }

};
```

:::{.callout-note title="Initial condition"}

The array `U` is expected to be populated with the initial concentration profile $U_i^0$ by the caller before the first invocation of `CNTimeStepping`. The module itself does not set or prescribe initial conditions.
:::

Since the movement of the agents is assumed to happen at very long time scales compared to $\Delta t$, we can update the concentration array `U` several times (`totalNumberOfIterations`) before updating their positions again in @lst-cn-set-parameters

## Summary

In this chapter we derived a Crank--Nicolson solver for the one-dimensional diffusion--reaction equation with point-like sources and sinks. The spatial discretization yields a tridiagonal linear system at each time step, which we solve efficiently using the Thomas algorithm. The module `crankNicolson.ts` exposes two functions: `CNSetParameters` to configure the solver, and `CNTimeStepping` to advance the concentration field in time.

The one-dimensional model is restricted to geometries that can be approximated as a filament or channel. In the next chapter we generalize the method to two spatial dimensions using the Alternating Direction Implicit (ADI) method, which reduces the two-dimensional problem to a sequence of one-dimensional tridiagonal solves along each coordinate direction.
